overview: This record follows Japan’s competing regional lords, the campaigns of Nobunaga and Hideyoshi, and the establishment of Tokugawa government. The atlas span, 1530 to 1650, starts after the civil wars began and continues well into the early Edo period. Its broad outline groups Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu together without showing rival domains; it does not mean a single government controlled them throughout. Hokkaido lies outside this imported outline.

periods.title: Regional lords and weakening shogunal rule
periods.summary: The atlas begins during prolonged conflict. Nobunaga expels the last Ashikaga shogun from Kyoto in 1573.

periods.title: Campaigns of unification
periods.summary: Nobunaga and then Hideyoshi extend central power. Ieyasu wins the decisive battle at Sekigahara in 1600.

periods.title: Early Tokugawa government
periods.summary: Ieyasu becomes shogun in 1603; the Toyotomi stronghold at Osaka falls in 1615.

periods.title: An early Edo continuation
periods.summary: The Tokugawa rebuild Osaka Castle from 1620. The atlas retains its older Warring States label until 1650.

sections.title: Unification changed government and people’s work

items.text: Regional military lords, known as daimyo, competed for territory while Ashikaga authority weakened. Nobunaga and Hideyoshi assembled much larger concentrations of power, and Ieyasu established the durable Tokugawa order. Their patronage also reshaped art: richly decorated castles announced the resources and ambitions of their owners.

Hideyoshi’s 1588 sword-collection order demanded that farmers surrender weapons, including firearms. It connected disarmament with reliable rent collection and preventing uprisings, while promising that farmers would prosper through cultivation. The decree reveals an effort to control rural society; it does not prove that every weapon was successfully collected.

Portuguese visitors brought matchlock firearms in 1543, and Japanese craftspeople soon produced guns themselves. Armourers also adapted European-style plate armour. These encounters changed workshops and military equipment, linking local skill to objects arriving by sea.

Unification at home did not end warfare abroad. Hideyoshi launched two devastating invasions of Korea, aiming ultimately at China. Trade and travel with neighbouring countries existed alongside these campaigns. The period’s celebrated castles and art belong to a history that also caused severe suffering beyond Japan.

sections.title: What a town’s rubbish can tell us

items.text: Excavations at Ichijodani recovered fish bones, shells, seeds and charred rice. Red sea bream bones retain knife marks from preparation. Food came from the sea, cultivated fields and wooded surroundings. Even after the meal was forgotten, a small cut on a bone could tell archaeologists that someone had been cooking.

One Ichijodani chopping board had previously been a wooden serving tray. The museum also displays ordinary lacquer bowls made with simpler, cheaper techniques than luxury pieces. Everyday cooking involved reused objects and affordable utensils, alongside the handsome vessels that usually attract attention in museums.

At the port town of Sakai, excavators found roads built from repeated layers of packed earth, with side drains for rainwater. Wells lined with specially made tiles appear from the sixteenth century. The lining helped prevent the sandy ground around the well from collapsing into the water supply.

Sakai’s excavated toilets often used unglazed jars buried with their mouths exposed. They stood beside streets, which the city’s archaeologists suggest made waste easier to collect for fertilizer. Even the least glamorous household container could have a second job helping crops grow.

Fire layers beneath Sakai preserve former streets and house plots. The city burned during the Osaka summer campaign of 1615, after which the Tokugawa laid out a larger town. Archaeologists distinguish this rebuilt area from the smaller trading community that had flourished before the destruction.

sections.title: Families and tea behind the castle walls

items.text: In a letter written from his headquarters in 1593, Hideyoshi told his wife One about diplomacy and military orders, then added that he had caught a cold. He also addressed Yodo-dono’s pregnancy with concern for One’s feelings. Affairs of state, illness and complicated family relationships could share a single sheet of paper.

The private upper enclosure of Hideyoshi’s Osaka Castle housed members of his family, including One, Yodo-dono and his son Hideyori. Its original stone walls were later buried during Tokugawa rebuilding; part was discovered in 1984. The later castle concealed an earlier household’s fortified setting below ground.

Himeji’s surviving early seventeenth-century castle combines timber buildings, white-plastered earthen walls, gates and interconnected defensive structures. Its elegant rooflines belonged to a working military headquarters. The white appearance earned it the name White Heron Castle, a peaceful-sounding nickname for a carefully defended place.

An early seventeenth-century black Raku tea bowl in the Metropolitan Museum was moulded by hand rather than shaped on a potter’s wheel. Such lightweight earthenware could be fired in small indoor kilns. Tea enthusiasts valued the rough, understated surface: impressive hospitality did not always require the shiniest cup.

sections.title: Books and a ruler’s written mark

items.text: In early seventeenth-century Kyoto, Saga editions gave older literature carefully designed covers, paper and illustrations. Their wooden printing type sometimes joined two to four characters in one piece, preserving the flowing effect of handwriting. Printing could multiply a book while still making its pages look elegantly written.

A 1608 printed Tales of Ise used a text descended from a copy Fujiwara Teika had made for his granddaughter in 1234. The National Archives preserves this illustrated edition. A family manuscript could help carry an older story into a new age of publishing, long after its first readers were gone.

A 1568 letter from Nobunaga confirms a man named Tohachi’s possession of rice fields. The museum cannot identify Tohachi more precisely. This small document shows another side of military authority: people needed written confirmation of the land on which wealth and livelihoods depended.

The letter bears 天下布武, read tenka fubu, in Nobunaga’s red seal. The museum renders it as “establishing military presence in the territory.” The characters here use modern type, not the seal’s carved lettering. Scholars debate how widely its word tenka extended: the slogan does not by itself prove a claim to rule the whole world.

ending.text: Tokugawa rule emerged before the atlas’s 1650 cutoff. Osaka Castle fell in 1615, ending the Toyotomi military challenge, and the Tokugawa rebuilt it from 1620. Japan’s regional societies, workshops and literary traditions continued under a new political order; the map’s old label outlasts the conflicts it describes.
